en: The Sūtra of the Bhikṣu Nāgasena, Volume One.
Translator’s name lost; appended to the Record of the Eastern Jin.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus. At that time, the various bhikṣus and...

There were more than ten thousand people in total—bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, ministers, elders, commoners, and those who followed the ninety-six types of paths—who daily listened to the sutras before the Buddha.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"The multitude of people grows daily, and my body finds no peace.
The Buddha desired to leave the multitude and go to a secluded place to sit and contemplate the Way.
The Buddha immediately left the assembly and entered the mountains, arriving among a thicket of trees.
That tree was possessed of a great deity; the Buddha sat beneath it and contemplated the Way.
Not far from the tree was a herd of five or six hundred elephants, among whom was an elephant king who was wise and knew both good and evil matters, appearing in form like a human being.
A great multitude of elephants surrounded the elephant king on all sides; the young elephants ran ahead of him, frolicking and plunging into the water, churning it until it became turbid and foul.
The young elephants again ran ahead, eating the choice grasses and trampling upon them as they played.
"My herd suffers greatly from many afflictions.

These elephants and their young calves stir up the water until it becomes turbid and foul, and they make the grass impure; yet, on the contrary, they constantly drink that turbid, foul water when hungry and eat the grass they have trampled underfoot."
The elephant king thought to himself,
"It would be pleasant for me to abandon these elephants and go to a secluded place!
The elephant king then abandoned the other elephants and departed, proceeding further into the mountains until he reached a grove of *tinduka* trees.

When the Elephant King saw the Buddha sitting beneath a tree, his heart was filled with great joy. He immediately approached the Buddha, bowed his head and knelt to pay homage to the Buddha, and then withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"I have left the multitude and come to stay among these trees; the elephant king has also left his herd and come to this same place among the trees—their circumstances are exactly the same."
The Buddha preached this sutra for the Elephant King, saying:
"Among humans, the Buddha is the most honored; among elephants, the Elephant King is the most honored.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"My mind and the mind of the elephant king are perfectly attuned; now I and the elephant king shall both enjoy ourselves together among these trees.
When the elephant king heard this sutra, his mind was immediately opened, and he understood the Buddha's intention.

The Elephant King then looked toward the place where the Buddha had been pacing back and forth, took water with his trunk and sprinkled it upon the ground, gathered grass with his trunk and swept the ground, and trod upon the earth with his feet to make it level and smooth.
The Elephant King said, "I have served the Buddha in this manner morning and evening.

After a long time, the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa; the Elephant King, not knowing where the Buddha was, traveled about searching for him. Failing to find the Buddha, he wept with falling tears, grieving and unhappy, unable to eat or drink.

At that time, there was a Buddhist monastery on a mountain in the kingdom called Karavāṇa Monastery. Within it resided five hundred śramaṇas who had all attained the path of arhatship; they regularly recited the sūtras until dawn on the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth days of every month.
At that time, the elephant king was also on the mountain, staying within the monastery.
Knowing that there would be a six-day recitation of the scriptures, the elephant king intended to go into the monastery on that day to listen to the teachings.
The śramaṇas knew the mind of the elephant king and listened to the sūtra; whenever they wished to recite the sūtra, they required the elephant king’s presence before they would recite.
The elephant king listened to the sūtra until dawn, neither sleeping nor lying down, remaining without movement or agitation.
Because the elephant king had frequently heard the sutras and served the Buddha, after his life came to an end and he died, he was reborn as a human being, born as a son into a brahmin family.

Later, as he grew older, having neither heard the Buddhist scriptures nor seen any śramaṇas, he abandoned his home and entered the deep mountains to study heterodox paths, making his dwelling upon a mountain peak.
Not far away, there was also a brahmin practitioner who lived together with him on the mountain; they frequented one another and shared a close friendship.
One of them thought to himself:
"I cannot escape the anxieties, sufferings, old age, and sickness of this world; after death, I shall surely enter the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and poverty."
"For this reason, I wish to shave my hair and beard, don the *kāṣāya*, and seek the path of Arhatship and *nirvāṇa*.
Then another person thought to himself:
"I wish to become a king and attain sovereign power, so that all the people of the world shall follow my commands."
After a long time had passed, the lives of both men came to an end, and they were both reborn in the world as commoners.
The one who had previously sought to become a king was born on the seashore as the crown prince of a king, named Milinda.

One of them, who in a previous life had desired to shave his head to become a śramaṇa and seek arhatship and nirvāṇa, was born in India with the name Tuolüe; he was born into his family together with a fleshly *kāṣāya* robe.
There was a great elephant born on the same day [as Nāgasena]; in India, elephants are called *nāga*, so his parents named him Nāgasena.

When he was fifteen or sixteen years old, he had an uncle named Lohan who had left the household life to study the Way as a śramaṇa. He possessed extraordinary talent that was peerless in the world; having attained the path of an Arhat, he could emerge from the Avīci hell and enter the Avīci hell, manifesting transformations at will and accomplishing anything. He knew in advance all that was thought in the minds of humans and gods, down to the smallest crawling insects, as well as where beings had come from in their past lives and where they would go after death.
Nāgasena went to his maternal uncle and said to him of his own accord:
"I take delight in the Buddha’s Way and wish to become a śramaṇa; I would serve as your disciple.
Would you permit me to become a śramaṇa?"
Lohan took pity on him and immediately permitted him to become a śrāmaṇera and receive the ten precepts.
He recited the sūtras daily and contemplated their teachings and precepts, whereby he attained the four dhyānas and came to fully understand the essentials of all the sūtras.
At that time, there was a Buddhist monastery in the kingdom named Ho-zen (Saṃghārāma). Within the monastery were five hundred śramaṇas, all of whom had attained the path of arhatship.
Among them was a foremost arhat named Ānanda, who was able to know the past, future, and present affairs of both the heavens and the human realm.
When Nāgasena reached the age of twenty, he received the sūtras and precepts of the Great Śramaṇa and went to the Saṅghārāma of Saṃghavardhana to visit Ānanda.
At that time, five hundred arhats had just gathered on the fifteenth day to recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Great Śramaṇa and were seated in the lecture hall.
The great śramaṇas all entered, and Nāgasena was among them; the śramaṇas all sat down.
Āṣāḍha said, "I have observed the minds of all the śramaṇas seated here, and they are all arhats; only Nāgasena has not yet attained arhatship."
Aṭṭhaka said: "It is like winnowing rice;
if there were black grains among the perfectly white rice, the winnowing would be considered unsuccessful.
Now, those in my assembly are all pure and white, and it is only Nātaputta who remains black, as he has not yet attained Arhatship."
When Nāgasena heard Āṣāḍha speak thus, great sorrow arose within him; he paid homage to the five hundred śramaṇas and departed.
He thought to himself:
"It is not fitting for me to sit among these seats, like a fox or a dog in the midst of a pride of lions."
"From this day forward, until I have attained the Way, I shall not enter and sit within it.
Ānanda, understanding Nāgasena’s intention, stroked Nāgasena’s head with his hand and said, "You will attain the path of Arhatship before long; do not be sorrowful."
He then detained Nāgasena.
Nāgasena had another teacher, eighty or ninety years of age, named Kāśyapa.
Among them was a very virtuous upāsaka who provided daily meals for Kāśyapa.
Nāgasena first took up the teacher’s alms bowl and went to fetch food; the teacher instructed Nāgasena to hold water in his mouth as they proceeded to the house of a lay follower to collect the meal.
The lay devotee saw that Nāgasena was young and handsome, far surpassing others; he was renowned, possessed vast and profound wisdom, was resolute, and was able to expound the scriptures and the Way.
When the upāsaka saw Nāgasena, he stepped forward, paid his respects, and with palms joined, said:

"I have provided meals for various śramaṇas for a long time, yet none of them has ever preached the sūtras to me. Now I beg Nāgasena for compassion; I pray that you will preach the sūtras to me and explain their meaning so that I may understand."
Nāgasena thought to himself:
"I have received my teacher's instruction and precept, which commands that I must not speak while water is held in my mouth.
If I were to spit out the water now, I would violate my teacher’s requirement."
"How should this be handled?
The lay follower Nāgapriya was also a man of high talent and great resolve.
[The Buddha thought: "If I preach the sutra for him, he will surely attain the Way."
Nāgasena then spat out the water, sat back down, and spoke this sutra for him:

"A person should practice giving to create merit and perform good deeds, and should reverently uphold the precepts of the Buddha’s sutras; after death, they will be reborn in the world as one who attains wealth and nobility."
"Those who do not violate the sutras and precepts will, in the future, no longer enter the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, nor fall into poverty; they shall attain rebirth in the heavens.
When the upāsakas heard Nāgasena’s exposition of the sutra, their hearts were filled with great joy.
The elder upāsaka, his heart filled with joy, then further preached the sutra for him, saying:
"All things in the world must pass away; there is nothing permanent."

All conditioned activities involve diligent toil, and all phenomena lack self-mastery; the path of Nirvana, however, is without birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, or affliction, for all evils and diligent toils are therein extinguished.
When Nāgasena had finished preaching the sutra, the lay follower attained the first stage of the path, that of a Srotāpanna; Nāgasena also attained the stage of a Srotāpanna.
The lay follower was greatly delighted and prepared an exquisite meal for Nāgasena with the utmost care.
Nāgasena said to the upāsaka:
"First take the eating utensils and place them in the teacher's bowl.
When Nāgasena had finished his meal and completed his rinsing and cleansing, he took the eating utensils and returned them to the teacher.
The teacher saw him and said,
"Today you have brought excellent provisions of food.
Because you have violated the community's agreement, you shall be expelled."
Nāgasena was deeply distressed and unhappy.
His teacher instructed him, saying:
"Convene the assembly of bhikṣus."
When they had all assembled and were seated, the teacher said:
"Nāgasena has violated the agreement of us all; he must be expelled and not allowed to remain among the assembly."
Āṣāḍha said, citing the Sūtra:

"It is like a person holding a single arrow who shoots and hits two targets; Nāgasena has attained the Way for himself and has likewise caused the upāsaka to attain the Way; he should not be expelled."
The teacher Kāśyapa said:
"Even if one were to shoot a hundred targets with a single arrow, one would still be offending many people; it simply cannot be stopped.
As for the others who uphold the precepts, they cannot equal Nātaputta in attaining the Way first. If you wish to emulate Nātaputta, you must cut off [the lineage] hereafter."
The entire assembly remained silent, and the teacher immediately expelled Nāgasena.

Nāgasena then prostrated himself at the teacher’s feet, rose, and after having paid homage to the entire community of bhikṣus, he departed. He entered the deep mountains and sat beneath a tree, where he practiced with diligence day and night, contemplating the Path without slackening. He spontaneously attained the state of an Arhat, gaining the powers of flying, seeing through, and hearing through; he knew the thoughts of others regarding good and evil, and he knew his own past lives and their origins.
Having attained the path of Arhatship, he returned to Huazhan Monastery and went before the bhikṣus; bowing his head to the ground, he repented his transgressions and sought reconciliation.
The community of bhikṣus immediately granted him permission.

After Nāgasena had paid his respects and departed, he traveled on through various commanderies, counties, streets, lanes, and alleys, preaching the sūtras and precepts for the people and instructing them in goodness. Among them, some received the five precepts; some attained the stage of *srotāpanna*; some attained the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*; some attained the stage of *anāgāmin*; and some became śramaṇas and attained the stage of *arhat*.

The second lord of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, Śakra Devendra; the seventh king of gods, Brahmā; and the fourth king of gods all came to where Nāgasena was, paid him homage by touching their heads to his feet, and withdrew to sit at one side. Nāgasena then preached the sūtras for the devas, and his fame spread far and wide.
Wherever Nāgasena traveled, the devas, humans, ghosts, spirits, and nāgas were all filled with joy upon seeing him, and they all obtained merit.
Nāgasena then proceeded to the kingdom of Śākya in India and stayed at the Kheḍaka Monastery.
There was a person known from a previous life who lived by the seashore; he was a prince of a kingdom named Milinda.

From his youth, Milinda had delighted in reading the scriptures and studying heterodox paths, coming to know all the doctrines and texts of those heterodox sects such that no follower of a heterodox path could defeat him.
When King Milinda’s father passed away, Milinda was established as king.
The king asked his ministers at his side:
"Among the ascetics and the people in the kingdom, who is capable of debating the difficult points of the scriptures and the Way with me?"
A border official reported, saying:
"There is one who studies the Way of the Buddha; people call him a śramaṇa.
His wisdom is subtle and penetrating, and he is able to debate the difficult points of the scriptures with Your Majesty."
"In the north is a great minister; his kingdom is named Śāketa, the palace of an ancient king. Within and without that country all is peaceful and secure, and the people are entirely virtuous.
Its city walls extend four directions with level paths for travel, and all its gates are carved and inlaid."

Furthermore, the other small kingdoms were mostly filled with men of high intelligence and brilliance. The people wore garments of five colors that shone brilliantly; the land was high and dry, abounding in rare treasures. Merchants from the four quarters conducted their buying and selling entirely in gold and silver coins. The five grains were plentiful and cheap, and every household possessed surplus livestock; the happiness there was beyond description.

King Milinda ruled the kingdom with the True Dharma; he was of high talent and possessed wisdom and strategic insight, being clear-sighted in administrative affairs. He was thoroughly proficient in the arts of warfare and could understand the ninety-six types of paths. His questioning was inexhaustible; as soon as someone spoke, he would already know their underlying intent.
The king said to his attendants,
"Is there among you any śramaṇa learned in the sūtras who can engage me in debate on the scriptures and discourse on the Way?
A minister of the king named Tiṃila-maṅgala addressed the king, saying:
"It is so. There is a śramaṇa named Yaśas who is learned in the scriptures and the Way, and is capable of debating the scriptures and the Way with Your Majesty.
The king then issued his command.
Chenmiliwangqun immediately set out to invite Yeheruo, saying:
"The Great King wishes to see the Great Master. Yeheruo replied:
"It would be most excellent if Your Majesty wished to see me.
Your Majesty should come in person; I shall not go.
Thus did Jāṃbūliṅga return and report to the king.
The king immediately mounted his carriage and, accompanied by five hundred musicians, proceeded to the monastery where he met Upagupta.
He went forward, exchanged greetings with him, and took his seat; the five hundred riders who followed him all sat down as well.
The King asked Yaśas:
"For what reason have you abandoned your home and forsaken your wife and children, shaving your head and beard and donning the *kāṣāya* to become a śramaṇa?
What path do you seek?"

Yasodhara said: "We study the Buddha-way and practice with rectitude; we obtain its blessings in this life and shall obtain its blessings in future lives as well. For this reason, we shave our hair and beards, don the kashaya robes, and become śramaṇas."
The King asked Vajjiputta:
"If there is a white-robed householder living at home with a wife and children who practices rectitude, will he obtain blessings in this present life and also obtain blessings in future lives?"

Vatsa said: "A white-robed householder who lives with a wife and children, yet conducts himself with uprightness, will obtain blessings in this present life and will also obtain blessings in future lives."
The king said, "Have you, sir,
abandoned your home in vain, forsaken your wife and children, shaved your head and beard, and donned the kashaya robe to become a śramaṇa?
Yasa remained silent and had no reply for the king.
The king’s attendants said to him, “This śramaṇa is one of great brilliance, wisdom, and insight; he was merely pressed for time and did not have the opportunity to speak.
All the king’s attendants then raised their hands and said:
"The King has won.
Yaśas was silent and accepted his defeat.
The King looked around at the upāsaka, but his face showed no sign of shame.
The king thought to himself:
"Among these upāsakas who show no shame on their faces, are there any other wise and capable śramaṇas who can engage me in debate?"
The King said to his attendant, Jāṃbūli:
"Is there any wise śramaṇa capable of debating the principles of the sūtras with me? Nāgasena was a master among the śramaṇas;

he understood the essentials of all the sūtras and was skilled in explaining the various distinctions, chapters, sections, and phrases of the twelve classes of scripture. He knew the path to Nirvāṇa, such that no one could exhaust him or defeat him. His wisdom was like the rivers and seas; he could subdue the ninety-six types of heterodox paths and was revered and loved by the disciples of the Buddha, teaching them through the principles of the sūtras.
Nāgasena arrived in the kingdom of Śāketa, accompanied by disciples who were all exceptionally brilliant; Nāgasena was like a fierce lion.
Jāṇussoni said to the king:

"There is a śramaṇa named Nāgasena, whose wisdom is subtle and profound, who possesses the essential points of all the sūtras and paths, who can resolve the doubts of others, and who is unimpeded in all things."
"You can indeed debate the Way with me in the *Nan jing* (Difficult Questions). The King asked Jianmi:
"Are you truly able to debate the Way with me in the *Nan jing*?"
Jāmbūli replied, “Indeed.
I constantly engage in difficult dialogues and discourse on the Way with the seventh Brahmā heaven, let alone with a king of men.”
He immediately commanded Jāṇussoni to go at once and invite Nāgasena to come.
Jāṇussoni went to Nāgasena’s location and said to him:
“The Great King wishes to see you.”
Nāgasena said, "Very well," and immediately accompanied by his disciples, he proceeded to where the king was.

Although the king had never seen Nāgasena before, as he walked among the crowd dressed in his robes, he was utterly distinct from others; seeing him from afar, the king recognized Nāgasena by his hidden qualities.
The king himself said:
"I have previously witnessed and entered many great assemblies, and though they were numerous, I never felt fear as I do today upon seeing Nāgasena."
"Today Nāgasena has surely defeated me; my heart is filled with trepidation and unrest.
Then Caṇḍagirika stepped forward and addressed the king, saying, "Nāgasena has already arrived this morning."
The king then asked Jāṇussoni, "Who is this Nāgasena?
Jāṇussoni replied and pointed him out to the king.
The king was immediately filled with great joy, thinking, "This is exactly what I had hidden in my mind.
Nāgasena arrived; the king rose to greet him with inquiries after his well-being, and being greatly delighted, he sat down together with him.
Nāgasena said to the king:
"The Buddhist scriptures state:

'For a person, peace and security are the greatest benefit; for a person, contentment is the greatest wealth; for a person, having faith is the greatest depth of character; and the path to Nirvana is the greatest bliss.'"
The king then asked Nāgasena,
"What is your name? Nāgasena replied:
"My parents named me Nāgasena, and people call me Nāgasena.
At times my parents call me Sīhanāda, and at times they call me Vijayaseṇa; it is for this reason that everyone recognizes me, as is common among people in the world."
The king asked Nāgasena, "Who is this Nāgasena?
The king asked again:
"Is the head Nāgasena? "It is not Nāgasena.
The King spoke again:
"Are the ears, nose, and mouth Nāgasena, or are they not?
The king spoke again:
"Is the chin, neck, shoulders, arms, hands, and feet Nāgasena?"
"It is not Nāgasena," [the king replied]. The king spoke again:
"Is it the thigh and leg that are Nāgasena?"
"It is not because of Nāgasena," the King said again.
"Is it because of his appearance, Nāgasena?"
“It is not Nāgasena,” the king replied again.
“Are suffering and pleasure Nāgasena?”
“It is not for Nāgasena,” [the King replied]. The King spoke again:
“Is it good and evil that constitute Nāgasena?”
"It is not Nāgasena," the king replied. The king spoke again:
"Is the body Nāgasena?"
"It is not Nāgasena," the king replied. The king spoke again:
"Are the liver, lungs, heart, spleen, intestines, and stomach Nāgasena?"
“It is not because of Nāgasena,” the king said again.
“Is it because of his appearance, Nāgasena?”
“Not for Nāgasena. “If suffering and pleasure, good and evil, and body and mind were combined, would that thing be Nāgasena?
Yet you say it is not Nāgasena?”
The king spoke again:
"If there is no suffering or pleasure, no complexion, no good or evil, and no body or mind—if these five things do not exist—could you truly be Nāgasena?"
Nāgasena said, "It is not for Nāgasena.
The King spoke again:
"Is it the sound of his voice and his breathing that makes him Nāgasena, or is it his speech?
What exactly constitutes Nāgasena?"
Nāgasena asked the king:
"What constitutes a chariot?
Is the axle the chariot?"
"It is not the chariot. Nāgasena said:
"Is the hub the chariot?"
The king said, "The hub is not the chariot. Nāgasena said:
"Are the spokes the chariot?
"They are not the chariot. Nāgasena said:
"Is the rim the chariot?
"It is not the chariot. Nāgasena said:
"Is the shaft the chariot?
"It is not the chariot. "Is the yoke the chariot?"
“It is not for the sake of the chariot. Nāgasena said:
“Is the carriage the chariot?”
"It is not for the sake of the chariot. Nāgasena said:
"Is it for the sake of the canopy?"
"It is not a chariot. Nāgasena said:
"If these pieces of timber were gathered together and placed on one side, would that be a chariot?"
"It is not for the sake of a chariot. Nāgasena said:
"Is it the sound that constitutes the chariot?"
“It is not for the sake of a chariot. Nāgasena said:
“What, then, constitutes a chariot?”
The king remained silent and said nothing.
Nāgasena said: "The Buddhist scriptures state:"
By assembling these various materials, one obtains a chariot through their use as causes;

a person is likewise so: by assembling the head, face, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, neck, shoulders, arms, bones, flesh, hands, feet, lungs, liver, heart, spleen, kidneys, intestines, stomach, complexion, voice, breath, and sensations of suffering, pleasure, good, and evil, they are combined to form a single person.
The king said, “Excellent, excellent! The king asked again:
"Nagasena, can you engage me in debate and discourse on the scriptures? Nagasena replied,
"If Your Majesty were to ask as a wise man, I would be able to answer Your Majesty accordingly."
"The questions of a king and the questions of a fool cannot be answered by one another.
The King asked, "What are the characteristics of the questions of a wise man, the questions of a king, and the questions of a fool?"

Nāgasena said: "The speech of the wise consists of responding to what is said, cross-examining, and using superior or inferior phrasing; when there is victory or defeat in speech, they know it for themselves—this is the speech of the wise."

When a king speaks with self-indulgence and audacity, such that anyone who dares to disobey or act contrary to his word is immediately subjected to forceful execution or punishment—this is called "the speech of a king."

The speech of a fool is such that when it is long, he cannot know it himself; when it is short, he cannot know it himself. He is obstinate and self-willed, seeking only victory; this is called the speech of a fool.
The King said: "I wish to employ the words of the wise, not the words of kings or fools.

Do not speak to me with the mindset of a king; rather, you should speak as you would to the śramaṇas, as you would to my disciples, as you would to the upāsakas, and as you would to my attendants; you should enlighten me."
Nāgasena said, "Very well. The king said:
"I wish to ask a question. Nāgasena said,
"Then let the King ask."
The king said, "I have already asked. Nāgasena replied:
"I have already answered," [the monk replied]. The king asked,
"What words did you say in answer to me?"
Nāgasena said: "What did I say when the King questioned me?
The King replied:
"I have nothing to ask," said Nāgasena. "I,
too, have nothing to answer."
The king immediately recognized that Nāgasena possessed great and brilliant wisdom.
The king said, "I have only just begun to ask many questions, yet the sun is already about to set; what shall we do?"
"Tomorrow we shall invite Nāgasena to the palace to engage him in questions regarding the marks of excellence. Jāṇussoni then said to Nāgasena:
"The sun is setting; the King will return to the palace, and tomorrow the King will invite you."
Nāgasena said, "Very well.
The king immediately paid homage to Nāgasena and, mounting his horse, returned to the palace, continuing to reflect upon Nāgasena throughout the journey.
On the following day, Chanmiliwangqun and his attendants addressed the king, saying:
"Should we invite Nāgasena?
The king replied:
"Please do so," [the king] said. Jāṃbuka replied:
"As for 'please,' how many śramaṇas should you send with him?"
The king said,
"How many śramaṇas did the independent Ājñātakauṇḍinya come with?
The treasurer, named Mātsarya, addressed the king, saying:
"Let Nāgasena come together with ten śramaṇas.
This was repeated up to three times, whereupon the king spoke with indignation:
"Why must you insist that Nāgasena come together with ten śramaṇas?"
The king said: "Your name is 'Miser.
You do not falsely claim that the king's property is your own; why then do you act contrary to my will?"
"There may indeed be grounds for punishment and retribution that can be spoken of.
How pitiable! I shall pardon your transgression.
Now that I have become a king, am I unable even to provide food for śramaṇas?"
Terrified by his great stinginess, he did not dare speak again.
Candraprabha went to Nāgasena, paid him homage, and said:
"The Great King invites you."
Nāgasena said: "How many recluses does Your Majesty wish for me to accompany?
Tiṣya-li-mo-wang-quen replied:
"How many śramaṇas does Pindola Bhāradvāja travel with?
At that time, Pindola was traveling together with eighty śramaṇas from the Vatsa country.
As Cāmali Wang Qunduan was about to enter the city, he encountered him on the road and asked Pindola:
"The other day, when I spoke with the King, you said there was no Nāgasena;
why was that? Nāgasena asked Caṅkī Māṭiputta:
"In your mind, what constitutes 'Nāgasena'?"
Jāṇussoni said: "I consider the breath, the inhalation and exhalation, to be Nāgasena. Nāgasena asked:
"If the vital breath has once departed and does not return, will that person ever live again? Zhānmílìwàngqún replied:
"One whose breath has departed and does not return is certainly dead."
Nāgasena said: "It is like a person blowing a reed flute; once the breath has gone out, it does not return.
Or, like a person holding a bellows for smelting gold and blowing a fire; when the breath has once gone out, can it ever return?"
Jāṇiśrī addressed the assembly, saying,
"I shall not return. Nāgasena said:
"The same breath has gone out and does not return; why, then, do people not yet die?
Zhānmílìwàng addressed the assembly, saying:
"I do not know what occurs during the interval between inhalation and exhalation; I pray that Naxian will explain this for us."
Nāgasena said: "The breath of inhalation and exhalation are all matters pertaining to the body.

Just as when the mind has something to think, the tongue speaks it—this is a matter of the tongue—and when the mind has something to doubt, the heart reflects upon it—this is a matter of the mind—each has its own presiding organ. When one looks at them from the perspective of emptiness, there is no Nāgasena."
When Zhānmílì saw that the hearts of the multitude were thus opened and resolved, he immediately became a lay follower (upāsaka) and received the five precepts.
Nāgasena then proceeded forward into the palace, arriving at the hall where the king was; the king immediately stepped forward to pay homage to Nāgasena and then withdrew.
Nāgasena sat down immediately, and the eighty śramaṇas all sat together with him. The king personally took beautiful food and placed it before Nāgasena.

When the meal was finished and the washing of hands was complete, the king bestowed upon each of the śramaṇas one piece of cotton cloth, one *kāṣāya* robe, and one pair of leather sandals; he bestowed three *kāṣāya* robes and one pair of leather sandals upon both Nāgasena and Vajjiputta.
The King said to Nāgasena and Yaśas:
"Let ten men remain together, and send all the others away.
Nāgasena immediately sent the other śramaṇas away and remained there together with the ten men.
The King commanded the ladies of the harem and the court musicians:
"All of you, come forth from the palace halls and listen within the curtains as I debate the Way of the Sutras with Nāgasena.
Then the ladies and musicians all came forth from the palace halls and listened within the curtains as Nāgasena preached the sutras.
Then the king took his seat before Nāgasena, and the king asked Nāgasena:
"What should one say when speaking of the Path? Nāgasena replied:
“If Your Majesty wishes to hear essential words, I shall speak those essential words.
The King said, “What do you sirs consider to be the most excellent path? For what purpose do you act as śramaṇas?”
Nāgasena said, “We of our class desire to cast off the suffering and afflictions of this world and no longer undergo the suffering and afflictions of future lives; therefore, we have become śramaṇas.
The King said:
"Are all śramaṇas like this? Nāgasena replied, "Not all become śramaṇas for this reason;
among them, there are those who become śramaṇas because they are in debt, those who become śramaṇas out of fear of government officials, and those who become śramaṇas because they are impoverished."

Nāgasena said: "I speak only of those who seek liberation from craving and the cessation of suffering; I do not refer to those who, though diligent and earnest in this life, have not yet attained the state of a śramaṇa."
The King asked,
"Is it for this reason that you have now become a śramaṇa?
Nāgasena replied:
“There is a small measure of the Buddha’s sūtras and the Way for those who become śramaṇas; therefore, I wish to renounce the suffering of this world and future worlds by becoming a śramaṇa.
The King said: “Excellent, excellent!”
The king asked, "Is there anyone who, after dying, is born again?
Nāgasena replied:
“Those who possess affection, love, and craving will be reborn as humans in future lives;
those who lack affection, love, and craving will not be reborn again in future lives.”
The king asked,
"If a person contemplates the True Dharma with a single-minded focus, will they not be reborn in future lives?
Nāgasena replied:
"If a person single-mindedly contemplates the True Dharma, wisdom, and other wholesome deeds, they will not be reborn in future lives.
The King asked:
"When a person contemplates the True Dharma with a virtuous mind and when one possesses clever wisdom—do these two matters have the same meaning?"
Nāgasena said, "Their meanings are each distinct and not the same.
The king said:
"Cattle, horses, and the six domestic animals each have their own wisdom and schemes;
their minds are not the same. Nāgasena said:
"Has Your Majesty ever seen those who reap wheat?"
"Holding grain in his left hand, he reaps it with his right. Nāgasena said,
"A wise person who cuts off craving and desire is like one who harvests grain."
The king said, “Excellent, excellent!
The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"What are these other virtuous deeds?
Nāgasena replied, "Sincerity and faith,
filial piety and obedience, diligence and mindfulness of the good, single-mindedness, and wisdom— these are virtuous deeds."
The King asked,
"What constitutes sincerity and trustworthiness? Nāgasena replied:
"Sincerity and faith resolve the doubts of people.

One must believe in the Buddha; believe in the Sūtras and the Dharma; believe in the existence of the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus; believe in the path of the Arhats; believe in this present life and believe in future lives; believe in filial piety toward one's parents; and believe that by performing good deeds one obtains good results, and by performing evil deeds one obtains evil results."
After one has faith in this, the mind becomes pure and departs from the five evils.
What are these five?
First, sexual lust; second, anger; third, indulgence in sleep; fourth, attachment to song and music; and fifth, doubt.
"If a person does not abandon these five evils, their mind will remain unsettled.
By abandoning these five evils, the mind becomes pure. Nāgasena said:
"It is like this: Suppose a Cakravartin King, with his chariots, horses, and retinue, crosses a river, causing the water to become turbid and foul.

Once they have crossed and departed, the king becomes thirsty and wishes to drink water. The king has a *maṇi* jewel; when it is placed in the water, the water immediately becomes clear, and the king is then able to drink the pure water."
Nāgasena said: "The human mind has five evils, like turbid water.
For the disciples of the Buddha who have crossed over the path of birth and death, the human mind is pure, like a pearl in clear water."
"A person who wards off all evils is sincere, trustworthy, and pure like a bright moon pearl.
The King said, "Excellent, excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"What is meant by 'diligence and sincerity'? Nāgasena replied:

"Among the various disciples of the Buddha, when they speak of their own purity within their respective ranks, some have attained the path of the Srotāpanna, some have attained the path of the Sakṛdāgāmin, some have attained the path of the Anāgāmin, and some have attained the path of the Arhat."
"By desiring to emulate [the sages] and practicing sincerity and faithfulness, one will then attain the Way that transcends the world. Nāgasena said:
"It is like a great rain falling upon a mountain; the water flows down in a vast torrent, and people on both sides, not knowing the depth of the water, are afraid and dare not go forward."

If there are people from distant regions who come to look at the water, he secretly knows its breadth, width, depth, and shallowness; knowing his own strength and capacity, he enters the water and successfully crosses over, and the crowds on both sides then follow him across.

The disciples of the Buddha are likewise; when the human mind is pure, one attains the path of the *srotāpanna*, the path of the *sakṛdāgāmin*, the path of the *anāgāmin*, and the path of the *arhat*.
Thus, through a virtuous mind and diligent effort, one attains the Way.
As the Buddha’s sutras state:
"If a person possesses a heart of sincerity and faith, they can attain deliverance by themselves."

If people of the world can restrain themselves from the five desires, recognize for themselves the suffering and affliction of the body, and achieve their own moral perfection through wisdom, they shall be able to liberate themselves.
The king said, "Excellent, excellent!
The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"What constitutes filial piety? Nāgasena replied,
"All that is wholesome constitutes filial piety."
Nāgasena said: "There are four wholesome states where the mind comes to rest. He continued:
“What are the four mental abidings? Nāgasena replied:

“First, observing one’s own body internally, externally, and both internally and externally; second, knowing the suffering and pleasure of the mind; third, knowing the goodness and evil of the mind; fourth, knowing the True Dharma. These are the four.”
Nāgasena said: "Furthermore, there are four things.
What are these four?"

First, to restrain one's intentions; second, not to allow any evil matters to enter the mind; third, to immediately expel evil matters from the mind as soon as they arise and to seek out all that is wholesome; fourth, to maintain and uphold whatever is wholesome within the mind without letting it go—these are the four.
Nāgasena said: "Furthermore, there are four things that one can do according to one's own will.
What are these four?"
"First is the rejection of desire, second is diligence, third is the restraint of the mind, and fourth is contemplation;
these are the four. Nāgasena said:
"Furthermore, there are five further tests."

What are these five? First is sincerity and faith; second is filial piety and obedience; third is diligence; fourth is exerting one's whole heart to contemplate what is good; and fifth is wisdom. These are the five.
Nāgasena said: "Furthermore, there are seven things that abandon all evils; they are called the Seven Virtues and are also known as the Seven Factors of Enlightenment.
There are also eightfold paths of practice, which are likewise called the Noble Eightfold Path."
"These thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are all rooted in filial piety. Nāgasena said:
"When an ordinary person carries gold a long distance to establish some achievement, it is entirely due to the earth that it is accomplished."
"Among the five grains and trees of the world that look toward the heavens, all grow from the earth.
Nāgasena said: "It is like a master builder who, intending to construct a great city, first measures out and establishes a foundation before raising the city."
Nāgasena said: "It is like a performer who, wishing to perform, first sweeps the ground clean before performing.

So too, a disciple of the Buddha seeking the Way first practices the Sūtras and the Precepts to cultivate wholesome causes; knowing the pains of diligent effort, he abandons all cravings and desires, and then contemplates the Eightfold Path."
The king said, "Excellent, excellent!
The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"What is meant by diligence? Nāgasena replied,
"Aiding what is wholesome is what constitutes diligence."
Nāgasena said: "It is like a wall about to collapse that one props up from the side, or a house about to fall into ruin that one likewise supports. Nāgasena said:

"It is like a king who dispatches troops to launch an attack; if the troops are few and weak and are about to be defeated, the king dispatches further troops to assist them, and they then achieve victory."

When a person possesses various evils, they are like having a weak army; when a person maintains a virtuous mind to eliminate an evil mind, it is like a king increasing his troops and achieving victory.
When a person upholds the five precepts, it is like gaining victory in battle.
"This is how diligence assists goodness in such a manner.
The Sūtra spoken by Nāgasena says:
"That which is assisted by diligence leads a person to the wholesome paths."
"Regarding the goodness thus attained, there is none that reaches this.
The King said, "Excellent, excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"What is meant by 'the mind should attend to all wholesome things'?
Nāgasena replied:
"It is like taking fragrant flowers and binding them together with thread; the wind cannot blow them apart.
Nāgasena spoke again:
"It is like a king's treasurer who knows exactly how much gold, silver, pearls, jade, lapis lazuli, and precious jewels there are in the treasury."
Nāgasena said: “When a practitioner of the Way seeks to attain the Way, he contemplates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

The mental orientation toward the Buddha-way should be correct in this manner: that is to say, the practitioner of the Way possesses an intention; by means of it, he knows good and evil and understands what ought to be practiced. He discriminates between the white and the black through reflection, and thereafter abandons evil and pursues good.”

Nāgasena said: "It is, for example, like a king who has gatekeepers; they know those whom the king respects and those whom he does not respect, and they know those who act to the king's disadvantage."
Those whom the honored and beneficial king admits within, he does not admit those whom he does not honor or who are not beneficial to him.
If a person maintains their mind in this way, they shall admit all that is wholesome and not admit all that is unwholesome.
"The mind controls human good and evil in this way.
Nāgasena spoke in a sutra, saying:
"A person should firmly guard their own mind and the six objects of desire of the body; by holding the mind very firmly, one will naturally attain the time of transcending the world."
The king said, “Excellent, excellent!
The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"What is that which is the one mind? Nāgasena replied:
"Among all wholesome states, the single mind is the most supreme."
"One whose mind is unified, all virtues follow him.
Nāgasena said: "It is like a staircase which must have something to lean against; likewise, all the paths of virtue are fixed upon a single mind."
Nāgasena said: "Suppose, for example, a king were to lead fourfold forces into battle—an elephant corps, a cavalry, a chariot corps, and an infantry.
When the king goes forth, all the troops follow, leading and following him from front and rear."
"In the Buddhist scriptures, all virtuous matters follow the single mind in this way.
Nāgasena spoke in the sutra, saying:
"The single mind is the sovereign of all virtues; though there are many practitioners of the Path, they should all return to the single mind."
"The birth and death of human beings in the past is like flowing water, where the preceding and succeeding moments follow one another.
The King said: "Excellent, excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again,
"What is wisdom? Nāgasena replied:
"I have already told the King that this man’s wisdom cuts through all doubts and illuminates all that is wholesome. Nāgasena said:
"It is like holding a lamp into a dark room; its darkness vanishes and it becomes bright by itself."
"Human wisdom is like this," said Nāgasena.
"It is as if a person were to take a sharp knife and cut wood; in the same way, one uses wisdom to cut away all evils."
Nāgasena said: "In this world, wisdom is the foremost; it delivers people from the path of birth and death.
The King said:
"Excellent, excellent!
The various teachings you have expounded from beginning to end are well-mastered through your wisdom.
The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"Is it only for the sake of pursuing desire and repelling all evil deeds that the Buddha's sutras exist?
Nāgasena replied, "Indeed."
"These various virtues that have been described are intended solely to eliminate all evils. Nāgasena said:
"It is like a king who mobilizes the fourfold army—elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry—to go into battle."
When first setting out on the path, the intention was merely to attack the enemy.
The Buddhist sutras describe various kinds of goodness in this same way: it is simply a desire to join forces in attacking and removing all evils.
The king said: "Excellent, excellent!
Your exposition of the sutra is most delightful."
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"When the human mind inclines toward the paths of good or evil and continues to sustain the body, is it the movement of this very spirit that gives rise to rebirth?
Or does another spirit arise and take birth?"
Nāgasena said: "It is neither the same as the former body and spirit, nor is it separate from the former body and spirit.
Nāgasena then asked the king:
"O King, when you were small and being nursed at the breast, and when you had grown to adulthood, was it not the same body that continued?
The King replied,
"The body in childhood was different."
Nāgasena said: "When a person is first in the mother’s womb as semen, until it reaches the state of being turbid—is it therefore still semen?
"It is different."
“When he was a child with firm flesh and bones, was it that same semen? “No.
“From the time of birth until the age of several years, was it that same semen? “No.”
“Different. “Suppose a person is practicing calligraphy; would a bystander ever be able to take over his skill?
The King said:
"One cannot substitute for his labor.
Nāgasena said: "It is like when a person commits a crime according to human law and informs the king; the king cannot understand or know [the crime] himself."
The king said, “If someone were to ask you, how would you explain it,
Nāgasena? Nāgasena replied:
"I have existed from childhood through youth until now; it is simply this same body that continues.
This large body and that small body constitute a single person, which is what life sustains."
Nāgasena asked the king, "Suppose a person lights a lamp; does it burn until daybreak?
The king replied:
"A person lights a lamp, and the oil lasts until dawn.
Nāgasena said: "Does the wick in the lamp continue to burn throughout the night because it is a continuous wick, or is it the flame that does not?"
"Is it because it is midnight or the time of dawn that the firelight does not shine?
The King replied,
"It is not because it is the firelight."
Nāgasena said: "When a lamp is lit, is it lit again from the first watch of the night until midnight?
Is it lit again at the time of dawn?"
The King said, "I did not light another fire at midnight; rather, I continued the single wick of fire until dawn. Nāgasena said:

"The human spirit continues in this way through successive succession: first it departs, then it returns; from the spirit until old age and death, the subsequent spirit proceeds toward its place of rebirth, continuing in successive succession. This is neither the same as the former spirit, nor is it separate from the former spirit."
"After a person dies, the spirit has a destination toward which it proceeds to be born.
Nāgasena said: "It is like when milk is turned into curd, and from the cream on top, clarified butter (ghṛta) is extracted."
“If one takes the froth from curd and butter and names it again ‘milk,’ would that person be able to use it?
The King said, “That person’s words cannot be used.”
Nāgasena said: "The human spirit is like milk.
From milk comes curd; from curd comes whey; from whey comes clarified butter (ghṛta); and from clarified butter comes the finest essence (sarpis).

In the same way, a person passes from the stage of embryonic fluid to birth, then to middle age; from middle age to old age, and then to death. After death, the spirit receives another body and is born again."
"When a human being dies, they shall again be reborn to receive another body, just as two wicks are lit one after the other.
The King said, "Excellent, excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"If a person is not reborn in a future life, can that person know for themselves that they will not be reborn?
Nāgasena replied:
"Indeed. There are those who can know for themselves that they will not be reborn in future lives.
The King said:
"What is the use of knowing this?
Nāgasena replied, "That person knows for themselves that they have no more affection, no more craving, and no more evils; by this self-knowledge, they know they will not be reborn in future lives."
Nāgasena asked the king:
"Suppose a farmer sows grain and harvests a great deal, filling his baskets and mats with the crop; if he does not plow or sow again the following year, would he still expect to obtain grain?"
The king said, "I no longer expect to obtain grain. Nāgasena said:

“The practitioner of the Way is also like this: having cast aside suffering and pleasure, as well as affection and love, they have nothing further to crave; therefore, they know for themselves that they will not be born again in future lives.
The King said: “Excellent, excellent!”
The king asked again:
"If that person will not be reborn in future lives, does he now possess any wisdom that differs from that of ordinary people?
Nāgasena replied:
"However, it differs from that of ordinary people.
The King asked:
"Are clarity and wisdom the same?"
Nāgasena said, "Clarity and wisdom are essentially the same.
The King asked:
"If a person possesses clear wisdom, can they fully know all matters, and by performing one task,
accomplish five tasks? Nāgasena replied,
"When one performs many tasks, that which is accomplished is not one."
It is like sowing grain in a single field: when they sprout, each produces its own kind.
So too, the five factors of the human body all rely on various conditions, each achieving its own specific result.
The king said, "Excellent, excellent!
The king then asked Nāgasena again:
“Worldly people all possess complete heads, faces, bodies, and four limbs; why then are there those with long lives and those with short lives?
Why are there those with many ailments and those with few ailments?”
Are there the poor and the wealthy?
Are there the noble and the lowly?
Are there those who are handsome and those who are ugly?
Among those conditioned by human existence, who is trusted by others and who is doubted by others?
Who is enlightened and who is in darkness? Why are they not the same?
Nāgasena said: "It is like various trees that produce fruit; some are sour, some are bitter, some are pungent, and some are sweet."
Nāgasena asked the king,
"For what reason are these trees not the same?
The king replied:
"As for their differences, their original seeds are each distinct. Nāgasena said:

"The actions performed by people are each different and not the same; therefore, there are those with long lives and those with short lives, those with many ailments and those with few ailments, the wealthy and the poor, the noble and the lowly, the handsome and the ugly, those whose words are heeded and those whose words are not heeded, and the wise and the ignorant."
Nāgasena said: "The Buddhist scriptures state that whether one is noble or poor, beautiful or ugly, all is obtained according to the good and evil deeds performed by oneself in previous lives."
The King said: "Excellent, excellent!
