King Fu asked Nāgasena again: "If a person wishes to perform good deeds, should they be performed beforehand or should they wait until later?"
Nagasena said:
"One should perform it while in front; that which is done afterwards does not benefit the person."
Nāgasena said: "When a king is thirsty, he digs the earth to make a well; can that well reach the thirst?
The King said:
"One cannot go to where one thirsts; rather, one should first dig a well.
Nāgasena said: "For this reason, that which is to be done must be performed beforehand."
Nāgasena asked the king,
“Does one have people plow and sow only when hungry, and wait until the grain has ripened before eating it?
The king replied:
"No. One must first provide for one's needs. Nāgasena said:
"A person should thus first perform good deeds; for one who performs good deeds only when in urgent distress, it will be of no benefit to themselves.
Nāgasena asked the king, "Suppose you have an enemy;
would you prepare your weapons for battle only when the time actually arrives?"
The King said, "No,
there must have been provisions stored beforehand. Nāgasena said:
“The Buddha spoke in a sutra, saying:
‘A person should first contemplate doing good for themselves; it is of no benefit to do good only afterwards.
Do not abandon the Great Way to follow deviant paths; do not emulate fools who abandon goodness to commit evil, for weeping in remorse later will be of no avail.’”
"Man abandons the upright and central path to follow what is not upright, only to feel regret at the moment of death.
The King said: "Excellent, excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"Your śramaṇas say that the fire of this world is not as hot as the fire in niraya (hell).

Yet they also say that if one places a small stone in the fire of this world, it will not be consumed until evening, whereas if one takes a large stone and places it in the fire of niraya, it is consumed immediately."
For this reason, I do not believe it.
Furthermore, you say that when a person commits evil, they die and dwell in the *niraya* hells for many thousands of millions of years, and that person does not die even then.
For this reason, I doubly do not believe these words.
Nāgasena asked the king,
"Have you ever heard of or seen great pythons, crocodiles, dragons, fish, or turtles that feed on sand and stones?
The king replied:
"Yes. Indeed, I take this as my food.
Nāgasena asked the king:
"Would sand and gravel ever be digested?
The King replied,
"They would all be digested."
Nāgasena asked, "If a woman carries a child in her womb, will it ever disappear?
The King replied:
"It will not be digested.
Nāgasena asked the king,
"Why will it not be digested?"
The King said, "It is because my fortune and merit alone are such that they cause [the offerings] not to be consumed. Nāgasena said:
“Regarding those in the hells who do not die even after tens of millions of years, what have they done?
It is because their transgressions and evils are not yet exhausted that they do not die. Nāgasena asked the king:
“Lions, tigers, and wolves all eat meat and bones; when they enter the belly, do they ever digest them completely? The King replied, “They do.”
Nāgasena asked the king,
"If a woman carries a child in her womb, does it ever disappear?
The king replied:
"It will not disappear," said Nāgasena.
"For what reason does it not disappear?"
The king said, "It is because of my unique ministerial rank and emoluments that death does not take me.
Nāgasena asked the king:
“Do oxen, horses, elk, and deer all feed on fodder?
The King replied,
“Indeed they do.”
Nāgasena asked: "Does that straw not indeed digest within the belly?
The King said:
"Everything is digested," said Nāgasena.
"But would that which is conceived within the womb be digested?"
The king said, "It cannot be digested. Nāgasena said:
"Why does it not digest?
The king replied,
"It is solely because of the natural course of my karmic fortune that it does not digest."
Nāgasena said: "It is the same for those in the hells; because their transgressions and evils are not yet exhausted, they do not die.
Nāgasena then asked the king:
“Worldly women eat all kinds of delicious food and consume it to their heart’s content; does it ever fail to digest within their bellies?
The King replied, “It all digests.”
Nāgasena asked, "If a woman carries a child in her womb, will it not be digested?
The King replied:
"The food does not digest," said Nāgasena.
"For what reason does it not digest?"
The King said,
"It is because my minister's salary is rightfully deserved that it does not diminish. Nāgasena said:
"Those within the hells are also like this; the reason they do not die for tens of millions of years is that because their prior evil deeds have not yet been exhausted, they do not die."
Nāgasena said: "A person is born in hell, grows old in hell, and only after the full duration has passed shall they die."
The king said, "Excellent, excellent!
The king then asked Nāgasena again:
“You śramaṇas, you say that the earth of the world rests upon water, the water rests upon wind, and the wind rests upon space.
I do not believe this.”
He then took the water from the king’s letter with his finger and, showing it to the king, asked:
"The wind holds the water in such a manner.
The king said:
"Excellent! The king asked Nāgasena again:
"Does the path to Nirvāṇa entirely pass away, so that nothing remains?"
Nāgasena said: "In the path of Nirvāṇa, nothing further exists. Nāgasena said:
"The foolish person covets and cherishes the body; for this reason, they are unable to attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Nāgasena said: "The wise person studies the Path; because they do not cherish the body internally or externally, they are free from affectionate attachment."

One who has no affection has no craving; one who has no craving has no womb; one who has no womb is not born; one who is not born does not age; one who does not age does not fall ill; one who does not fall ill does not die; one who does not die has no sorrow; one who has no sorrow does not weep; one who does not weep has no pain, and thus attains the Way of Nirvana.
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"Can all those who practice the Way attain the path of Nirvāṇa?
Nāgasena replied:
"One cannot fully attain the path to Nirvāṇa.

Those who are rightly oriented toward the good path must learn to know what is right: they should practice that which ought to be practiced and abandon that which ought not to be practiced; they should contemplate that which ought to be contemplated and discard that which ought not to be contemplated. In this way, one can attain the path to Nirvāṇa."
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"As for those who have not attained the path of Nirvāṇa, do they know that the path of Nirvāṇa is blissful?
Nāgasena replied:
"It is so. Although one has not yet attained the path to Nirvana, it is indeed a joy to know the path to Nirvana.
The King said:
"If a person has not yet attained the path of Nirvāṇa, by what means can they know its bliss?
Nāgasena asked the king,
"When a person has never before had their hands or feet cut off, how could they know whether having one's hands and feet cut off would be a most excruciating pain?"
The King said,
"Although I have never before had my hands or feet cut off, I still know what it means to be in pain. Nāgasena said:
"What is the use of knowing what pain is?
The King replied, "I see a person with their hands and feet severed, groaning and crying out; it is for this reason that I know what pain is."

Nāgasena said: "In the presence of others, there are those who have attained the path to Nirvāṇa; they speak to one another of how delightful the path to Nirvāṇa is, and for this reason, people believe it.
The King said:
"Excellent, excellent!
The king asked Nāgasena again,
"Have you ever seen the Buddha?"
Nāgasena said, "I have never seen it. The King said:
"Nagasena, have your teachers ever seen the Buddha? Nagasena replied,
"Your teachers have likewise never seen the Buddha."
The King said: "If Nāgasena and the other masters have not seen the Buddha, then it must be that the Buddha does not exist.
Nāgasena replied:
"Great King, have you ever seen the place where five hundred mountain streams converge? The King replied, "I have not."
“Did your grandfather and great-grandfather both see the water?
The king replied, “Neither saw it.”
Nāgasena said: "Your father and grandfather did not see this water; does that mean it is certain that there is no place in the world where these five hundred mountain streams converge?"
The king said,
“Although I have not seen it, and neither my father nor my grandfather saw this water,
this water truly exists. Nāgasena said:
"Although neither I nor our teachers have seen the Buddha, in truth there is a Buddha.
The king asked again:
"Is there anyone superior to the Buddha?"
Nāgasena said: "Indeed.
There is none superior to the Buddha."
The King asked again:
"In what way is there no one who can surpass the Buddha?
Nāgasena asked the King:
"Suppose there is a person who has never entered the great ocean; how could they know whether the seawater is vast?
There are five rivers, and each river has five hundred small tributaries flowing into it."
There are five rivers: the first is named Gaṅgā, the second Sindhū, the third Vakṣu, the fourth Śatadru, and the fifth Vitastā.
These five rivers flow into the ocean day and night, yet the waters of the ocean neither increase nor decrease.
Nāgasena said: "O King, can you hear and know? The King replied:
Nāgasena replied, "I know it truly.
Because those who have attained the Way speak of the Way together, and there is no one capable of surpassing the Buddha, for this reason I believe him."
The king said, “Excellent, excellent!
The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"What need is there to know that there is no Buddha superior?
Nāgasena asked the king:
"Who was the teacher who created writing?"
The King said,
"The name of the scribe who created the script is Tissa. Nāgasena said:
"Your Majesty, have you ever seen Citta?
The King replied, "Citta died long ago; I have never seen him."
Nāgasena said: "Your Majesty has not yet seen the original draft; how do you know that the draft was made by the scribe? The King said:
"By means of the written characters of ancient times, which have been transmitted and taught to one another, I know that this is called 'substance' (*dravya*). Nāgasena said:
"For this reason, when we see the Buddha’s sūtras and precepts, it is no different from seeing the Buddha himself."

The sūtras and the Way taught by the Buddha are exceedingly profound and sublime; once people have come to know the Buddha’s sūtras and precepts, they subsequently emulate them. For this reason, I know that there is no one who can surpass the Buddha.
The King asked Nāgasena again,
"Having seen the path of the Buddha's scriptures for myself, can it be practiced for a long time?
Nāgasena replied:
“The Sūtra on the Precepts and Prohibitions taught by the Buddha is most excellent; we shall uphold and practice them until old age.
The King said: “Excellent, excellent!”
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"After a person has died, does the body not follow them into rebirth in a future life?
Nāgasena replied:
"Once a person has died, they receive a new body; therefore, the old body does not follow. Nāgasena said:
"It is like the wick of a lamp, which is continuously lit one after another; thus the old wick remains while a new wick is lit in its place."
"The human body is likewise: when the present body does not practice [the Way], one receives a new body.
Nāgasena asked the king:
"When you were young, did you follow a teacher to study writing and read the scriptures?"
The king said, “Indeed.
I shall continue to keep it in mind.”
Nāgasena asked the king:
"Regarding the teacher from whom Your Majesty received the scriptures, does that teacher know the original scriptures?
Have you not acquired all those original scriptures from him?"
The king said, “No.
My teacher merely knows the original scriptures himself.”
Nāgasena said: "The human body is like this: one discards the old body and receives a new one.
The King said:
"Excellent, excellent!
The king asked Nāgasena again,
"Is it certain that there is wisdom, or not?"
Nāgasena said: "There is no wisdom [in that].
For example, suppose a person steals another's fruit; would the thief not have committed an offense?"
The king said, "There is a fault. Nāgasena said:
“When one first plants a tree, there are no fruits upon it; for what reason, then, would the thief be at fault?
The King said, “If one does not plant the tree, for what reason would there be any fruit?”
"Therefore, the thief has no fixed form. Nāgasena said: "A person is also like this;
having performed good or evil deeds with the body of this life, one is born in a future life and receives yet another new body."
The King said,
"It is because of this that people perform good and evil deeds with their bodies.
Nāgasena replied:
"The good and evil deeds performed by people follow them like a shadow follows the body.
When a person dies, only their physical form perishes, but their actions do not perish.
It is like writing at night by the light of a fire; when the fire is extinguished, the characters remain, and when the fire returns, they are once again made manifest."
"What one performs in this life will be realized in the next life; one receives its fruit accordingly.
The King said: "Excellent, excellent!"
The King said to Nāgasena,
"Can you distinguish and point out where good and evil reside?
Nāgasena replied:
"It is impossible to know where good and evil reside.
Nāgasena asked the king:
"When trees have not yet borne fruit, would you be able to distinguish and point out, saying that there is such-and-such fruit on this branch and no fruit on that branch?"
"Is it possible to know this beforehand?
The king replied,
"It cannot be known."
Nāgasena said, "A person who has not yet attained the Way cannot know in advance where good and evil reside.
The King said:
"Excellent, excellent!
The king asked again:
"When a person is to be born in a future life, can they know it for themselves?"
Nāgasena said, "Those who are to be born know it themselves.
The King said:
"What is the use of knowing this?
Nāgasena replied, "Suppose a farmer plows and sows his fields; when the rains come at the proper season, can that man know with certainty beforehand whether he will obtain grain?"
The king said, "Indeed,
I know this. I know that by tilling the field, one shall obtain much grain."
Nāgasena said, "In this way,
a person will be reborn in a future life and know it beforehand.
The King said:
"Excellent, excellent!
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"Is there truly nirvāṇa, or is there not?"
Nāgasena said, "Indeed they exist.
The King said to Nāgasena:
"Could you point out to me where the Buddha is? Nāgasena replied,
"One cannot point out the location of the Buddha."
"The Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa; it is impossible to point out where he may be seen. Nāgasena said:
"Suppose, for example, a person were to kindle a great fire and then immediately extinguish its flames; would it still be possible to point out and know where the light remains?"
The king said, "It cannot be known. Nāgasena said:
"The Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa; his whereabouts can no longer be known.
The king said, "Excellent, excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"Can a śramaṇa truly love his own body?
Nāgasena replied:
“The śramaṇa does not love his own body.
The king said,

“If it were the case that the śramaṇa did not love his own body, for what reason would he regulate himself through rest and sleep, desire peaceful and warm food and drink, and desire to protect and care for himself with excellence?”
"Why is that? Nāgasena asked.
"Has Your Majesty ever entered into the midst of battle?"
The king said, "Indeed.
I have once entered into the midst of battle."
Nāgasena asked, "When you were in the midst of battle, were you ever struck by the wounds of sword-blades, spears,
or arrows? The King replied:
"I have been struck by the edge of a blade.
Nāgasena asked the king,
"What do you do with the wound from the blade's edge or the arrow-head?"
The king said,
"I have wrapped my ear with cotton soaked in medicinal ointment.
Nāgasena asked the king:
"Is it because you love the ulcer that you wrap it with medicinal ointment, cotton,
and silk floss? The King replied,
"I do not love the ulcer."
Nāgasena said, "If one truly does not love a wound, why does one apply medicinal ointment and wrap it with cotton wool to protect it?
The King said:
"I wish for this wound to heal quickly.
Nāgasena said, "The śramaṇa is just like this."

He does not cherish his own body; even when eating and drinking, his mind finds no pleasure in making them delicious or beautiful, nor in enhancing their color and texture, but seeks only to sustain the physical frame so as to uphold the precepts of the Buddha’s sutras.
The Buddhist scriptures state that a person has nine apertures which are like nine arrow-wounds, and all these apertures are foul-smelling and impure.
The King said: “Excellent, excellent!”
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"Does the Buddha possess a body with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, all golden in color and endowed with a halo?"
Nāgasena said, "The Buddha truly possesses a body with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, all of which are enveloped in a golden radiance.
The King said:
"Does the body of the Buddha’s parents possess the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, and is it entirely golden in color with a halo of light?
Nāgasena replied,
"The Buddha’s parents do not possess these marks."
The king said,
"Regarding such marks and signs, my parents do not possess them, nor does the Buddha possess them.
The king spoke again:
"A child takes after its kind; if the parents do not possess these marks, the Buddha certainly does not possess them. Nāgasena said:
"Although the Buddha’s parents did not possess these thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, nor that golden hue of the body, the Buddha truly possesses these marks."
Nāgasena said: "Has Your Majesty ever seen a lotus?
The King replied:
"I have seen it. Nāgasena said:
"This lotus flower grows from the earth and matures in mud and water."
"Is its color not exceedingly fine? Does it bear any resemblance at all to the color of mud and water?
The King replied, "It does not resemble the color of earth, mud, or water."
Nāgasena said: "Although his parents did not possess these marks, the Buddha truly possessed them.
Though the Buddha was born into the world and raised in the world, he did not conform to worldly ways."
The king said, "Excellent, excellent!
The king then asked Nāgasena again:
“Is it true that the Buddha, just like the seventh heavenly king Brahmā, does not engage in sexual intercourse with women?
Nāgasena replied, “Indeed, it is so.”
"He has thoroughly distanced himself from women; he is pure and free from blemish.
The King said, "If the Buddha were to act as the Seventh Heavenly King does, the Buddha would be a disciple of the Seventh Heavenly King Brahmā."
Nāgasena asked the king,
"Does the King of the Seventh Heaven possess mindfulness or not?
The king replied:
"The seventh heavenly king, Brahmā, possesses mindfulness. Nāgasena said:
"For this reason, the seventh heavenly king Brahmā and all the higher deities are disciples of the Buddha."
Nāgasena asked the king,
"What kind of sound is it when an elephant cries?
The king replied:
"The elephant's cry is like the cry of a goose.
Nāgasena said: "If that were so, would the elephant then be a disciple of the goose?"
"Are they each of different kinds?
"The Buddha is likewise; he is not a seventh-heaven king nor a disciple of Brahmā.
The king said:
"Excellent, excellent!
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"Does the Buddha know all the sūtras and precepts through study?"
Nāgasena said: "The Buddha has fully studied, known, and practiced the sūtras and the precepts.
The King asked:
"From whom did the Buddha receive the sūtras and precepts as his teacher? Nāgasena replied,
"The Buddha had no teacher."
When the Buddha attained the Way, he spontaneously and fully knew all the paths of the various sutras.
Unlike the disciples who must learn through study, all the disciples taught by the Buddha should practice and uphold his instructions until old age.
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"When the parents of a person die, they weep and shed tears; when a person hears the Buddha’s sūtras, they likewise weep and shed tears. Are these two cases not identical?"
Nāgasena said: “When people weep for their parents, it is because they feel gratitude and affection for their kindness, and they grieve with sorrow and distress over them.

The grief of such people is the grief of the ignorant. However, when those who have heard the Buddha’s sūtras and the Way shed tears, it is because they possess a heart of compassion and pity, mindful of the diligent suffering of the world; for this reason, they shed tears.”
"The merit one gains from this is exceedingly great. The King said, "Excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"What is the distinction between those who have attained liberation?
Nāgasena replied:
"Those who have not yet attained liberation possess a mind of craving; those who have attained liberation possess no mind of craving, desiring only to seek food and drink to sustain their lives."
The King said:
"I see that all people in the world desire physical comfort; they seek fine food without ever feeling satisfied.
Nāgasena replied:
"Those who have not yet attained liberation consume food and drink for the sake of honor, pleasure, and fine delicacies.
Those who have attained liberation, though they eat and drink, do not regard it as pleasure nor as something sweet; they do so merely to sustain their lives."
The king said, "Excellent, excellent!
The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"Can people, when engaged in some activity, recollect events from long ago?
Nāgasena replied,
"When people are in a state of sorrow or anxiety, they all recollect events from long ago."
With what does the King contemplate this?
Does he do so through focused mindfulness (*cetanā*),
or through moment-to-moment mindfulness (*smṛti*)?
Nāgasena asked the king:
"Have you ever learned or known something and later recalled it?
The king replied:
"Yes. There was something I once learned and understood, which I have since suddenly forgotten," said Nāgasena.
“Was it that Your Majesty had no intention at that time, or did you simply forget?
The King replied,
“At that time, I forgot my mindfulness.”
Nāgasena said: "It can be compared;
Your Majesty possesses elephants.
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"Does every action a person performs involve mindfulness?
When one first begins to act, does one perceive the present action through mindfulness?
Nāgasena replied:
“One knows all past matters by means of mindfulness, and one also knows present matters by means of mindfulness.
The king said,
“Such a person merely recollects past matters and is unable to recollect new matters.”
Nāgasena said: "Even if something new were to be produced, that which cannot be recollected would be just like this.
The King said:
“Is it that for a person newly learning the arts and techniques, their effort is in vain?

Nāgasena replied, “When a person newly learns calligraphy or painting, because they possess mindfulness (*smṛti*), they cause the disciples who learn from them to understand; therefore, it is precisely because of mindfulness.”
The king said, "Excellent, excellent!
The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"By how many things does a person give rise to successive thoughts?
Nāgasena replied,
"A person generally gives rise to thoughts by means of sixteen things."

First, the arising of mindfulness regarding what was done long ago; second, the arising of mindfulness regarding what has newly been learned; third, the arising of mindfulness regarding the occurrence of a major event; fourth, the arising of mindfulness through reflecting on the wholesome; fifth, the arising of mindfulness regarding previously experienced suffering; sixth, the arising of mindfulness through self-reflection; seventh, the arising of mindfulness regarding previously mixed actions; eighth, the arising of mindfulness through teaching others; ninth, the arising of mindfulness regarding elephants; tenth, the arising of mindfulness regarding something previously forgotten; eleventh, the arising of mindfulness due to recognition; twelfth, the arising of mindfulness through calculation; thirteenth, the arising of mindfulness regarding debt; fourteenth, the arising of mindfulness through single-mindedness; fifteenth, the arising of mindfulness while reading books; sixteenth, the arising of mindfulness upon seeing again something that was previously entrusted to one.
"These are the sixteen matters that give rise to mindfulness.
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"What constitutes long-standing mindfulness?"

Nāgasena said: "The Buddha’s disciple Ānanda had a female disciple, the laywoman (upāsikā) Kūṭadantī, who could recollect the events of a thousand koṭis of past lives; furthermore, other practitioners of the Way are all able to recollect matters of the past."
"Just as Ānanda has a great many female disciples, having thought this, he then gave rise to a thought.
The King asked again:
"What kind of new thoughts have arisen?"
Nāgasena said: "It is like a person who once studied and learned how to calculate, but later forgot it;
upon seeing someone else calculating, he then gives rise to the thought again."
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"What is it that gives rise to the thought of great matters?
Nāgasena replied:
"It is like a crown prince who, upon being established as king, thinks to himself, 'I am now noble and eminent'; this is the arising of a thought born of a great matter.
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"What is it that gives rise to a thought when one contemplates what is wholesome?"
Nāgasena said: "Suppose, for example, a person is invited by another and is treated with the utmost kindness, courtesy, and hospitality.
That person thinks to himself:"
"In the past, when I was summoned by someone, I treated them with a kind heart; this is what is meant by 'generating thoughts through reflection on the good.
" The King then asked Nāgasena:
"What is meant by 'generating thoughts through reflection on further suffering'?"
Nāgasena said: "It is like a person who has once been beaten by others and imprisoned; this gives rise to the thought of renewed suffering.
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"What is meant by 'giving rise to a thought through self-reflection'? Nāgasena replied:
"It is, for example, like a person who has previously seen their family, kinsmen, or domestic animals; this is what is meant by giving rise to a thought through self-reflection."
The king asked Nāgasena again,
"What is meant by 'a thought arising from that which was previously mixed with action'? Nāgasena replied:

"It is like a person who contemplates the names, forms, colors, fragrances, odors, sourness, and bitterness of the myriad things; to contemplate these various matters is what is meant by 'having previously given rise to mixed thoughts.
The King asked Nāgasena again, "What is it that causes a person to give rise to thoughts?"
Nāgasena said: "People naturally delight in forgetting others; among them, some may remember and some may forget, so this teaching is intended to give rise to mindfulness in people.
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"What is meant by 'the elephant's recollection of its origin'?
Nāgasena replied, "Humans, oxen, and horses each have their own kind of elephant; this is what is meant by 'the elephant's recollection of its origin'."
The King asked Nāgasena again,
"What is it that one has forgotten yet subsequently recalls?
Nāgasena replied:

“It is like a person who has suddenly forgotten something; by thinking of it repeatedly and alone, they recover it. This is what is meant by ‘the arising of thought from that which was previously forgotten.
The King asked Nāgasena again:
“What is the cause for the arising of thought from consciousness?”
Nāgasena said: "One who studies writing can arrange its characters in sequence; this is how consciousness gives rise to mindfulness.
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"What is meant by 'giving rise to thoughts through calculation'?

Nāgasena replied, "It is like people engaging in calculation together; when they have mastered it so as to know everything and their skillful methods are clear, this is called giving rise to thoughts through calculation."
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"Who is it that gives rise to the thought of being in debt?
Nāgasena replied:
"Just as when a person owes a debt that must be repaid, this is what is meant by 'giving rise to the thought of being in debt.
The King then asked Nāgasena:
"What is it to give rise to the thought with a single-minded focus?"
Nāgasena said: "The śramaṇa unifies his mind and recollects the events of a thousand billion lifetimes from which he has come; this is what I mean by 'unifying the mind to produce recollection.'"
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"What is meant by one who recites and remembers what they have read? Nāgasena replied:

"The Emperor possesses ancient books; when he reflects and says, 'This was the record of such-and-such an Emperor or such-and-such an official at that time,' this is what is meant by generating recollection through reading books.
What is it that, having once been entrusted to memory, gives rise to further recollection?"

Nāgasena said: "If a person has something entrusted to them and sees it again with their own eyes, they then give rise to a memory; this is what is called 'giving rise to a memory based on that which was entrusted. The King said:
"Excellent, excellent!
the king said again, and he asked Nāgasena:
"Does the Buddha know all things that have already passed and those that are yet to come?"
Nāgasena said, "Yes. The Buddha knows all."
The king said:
"If the Buddha knows all matters completely, why does he not instruct his disciples all at once? Why does he instruct them gradually?"
Nāgasena asked the king,
"Does there not happen to be a physician in the kingdom?
The king replied:
"There is a physician," Nāgasena said.
"Is that physician able to know all the medicines in the world?"
The king said,
“I can know all medicinal herbs.
Nāgasena asked the king:
“The physician who treats people’s illnesses—does he give them medicine all at once, or does he give it to them gradually?
The King replied, “One cannot give medicine in advance when one is not yet ill; one gives medicine only when there is an illness.”

Nāgasena said: "Although the Buddha fully knows all matters of the past, future, and present, he cannot instruct all the people of the world at once; rather, he must gradually bestow the sūtras and precepts so that they may practice them."
The King said, "Excellent, excellent!
The King then asked Nāgasena again:

"You śramaṇas say that if a person commits evil throughout their life in this world for as long as a hundred years, yet at the moment of death they recollect the Buddha, then after death they will all be reborn in the heavens."
"I do not believe these words.
Furthermore, you say that upon killing a single living being, one immediately enters hell;
I do not believe this either."
Nāgasena asked the king, "Suppose a person were to take a small stone and place it upon the water; would the stone float or sink?
The king replied:
"The stone has sunk," [the King said].
Nāgasena replied, "Suppose one were to place a hundred large stones upon a boat; would that boat sink?"
The King said, "It does not sink. Nāgasena said:
"Just as a hundred large stones in a boat do not sink because of the boat, so too,
though a person may possess inherent evil, by reciting the Buddha's name for a single moment, they will not enter the hells but will instead be reborn in the heavens."
"As for those small stones that sank, they are like people who commit evil and do not know the Buddhist scriptures; after death, they enter the hells.
The King said, "Excellent, excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"For what purpose do you practice the Way and become śramaṇas?
Nāgasena replied:
"Out of a desire to abandon these sufferings—past suffering, present suffering, and future suffering—and not wishing to undergo them again, I practice the Way and become a śramaṇa."
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"If suffering occurs only in future lives, why do you study the Way and become a śramaṇa beforehand?
Nāgasena asked the King:
"Does Your Majesty perhaps have an enemy state or a hostile kinsman who wishes to attack you?
The King replied, "Indeed."
"There is an enemy kingdom whose people constantly desire to attack one another.
Nāgasena asked the king:
"When the enemy lord was about to arrive, did Your Majesty prepare weapons for battle and dig defensive moats?"
"Should one prepare for this in advance?
The King replied,
"One ought to have provisions stored in advance."
Nāgasena asked the king,
"For what reason do you first make provisions?
The king replied:
"Because one must be prepared for the enemy's arrival at any time.
Nāgasena asked the king, "The enemy has not yet arrived; why do you prepare for him in advance?"
Nāgasena asked the king again:
"When hungry, one plants in the fields; when thirsty, one digs a well. For what reason do you prepare such provisions in advance?
The king replied:
"Excellent, excellent!
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"How far is the seventh Brahmā heaven from here?"
Nāgasena said: "It is very far.
Suppose one were to drop a stone as large as a royal palace from the seventh Brahma heaven; it would take six days for it to fall to this earth."
The king said,
"You śramaṇas claim that you have attained the path of arhatship and can fly up to the seventh Brahma-heaven in the time it takes a person to bend and stretch their arm."
The king said, "I do not believe this.
Having traveled many thousands of millions of li, how can it be so swift?"
Nāgasena asked the king,
"In what country was Your Majesty born?
The king replied:
"I was originally born in the country of Da Qin; its name is Alisān.
Nāgasena asked the king, "How many *li* is it from here to Alisān?"
The king said,
"It is two thousand yojanas from here, which makes eighty thousand li.
Nāgasena asked the king:
"Have you ever, while at a distance from here, thought back to the affairs of your own kingdom?
The King replied, "Indeed."
"I am merely constantly thinking of matters from my own country.
Nāgasena said, "Your Majesty,
try once more to think of something you did while in your own country?"
The king said, "I have already thought upon it. Nāgasena said:
“The King travels eighty thousand *li* to and fro; how can he do so so swiftly?
The King replied, “Excellent, excellent!”
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"Suppose two people were to die here together; one would be reborn in the seventh Brahma-heaven, and the other would be reborn in Kaśmīra."
"Kashmir is seven hundred and twenty *li* away; who was the first to arrive there?
Nāgasena replied, "Try thinking of the country of Aḷaka."
The king said, "I have already considered it.
Nāgasena spoke again:
"Your Majesty, please try again and think of Kaśmīra. The King said,
"I have already thought of it."
Nāgasena asked the king,
"Of these two countries, which one do you consider more urgent?
The king replied:
“They are exactly the same,” Nāgasena replied.
“When two people die together, one is reborn in the seventh Brahma-heaven and the other is reborn in Kaśmīra; they are likewise equal.”
Nāgasena asked the king:
"Suppose there were two birds flying together; one perched on a high tree and the other on a low tree. As both birds fly away, whose shadow would reach the ground first?"
The king said,
"Their shadows both reach the ground. Nāgasena said:
“Both have died; one has been reborn in the seventh heaven and the other in Kaśmīra, and they have both arrived at the same time.
The King said, “Excellent, excellent!”
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"By how many means does a person learn to know the Way?
Nāgasena replied:
"By means of seven matters, one learns to know the Way.

What are these seven? First, mindfulness of good and evil deeds; second, diligence; third, delighting in the Way; fourth, subduing the mind to do good; fifth, mindfulness of the Way; sixth, single-mindedness; seventh, being appropriately free from both hatred and attachment."
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"Does a person learn the Way by means of these seven things?
Nāgasena replied:
"One does not know the Path by learning through all seven matters.
One who knows maintains that knowledge of good and evil; it is by means of this one matter alone that one distinguishes and knows.
The King then asked Nāgasena:
"If one were to know by means of a single matter, why did you speak of seven matters?
Nāgasena asked the king, "Suppose a person takes a sword and places it in its scabbard leaning against a wall; would that sword be able to cut anything on its own?"
The king said, "I cannot cut or sever anything. Nāgasena said:
"Although the human mind is luminous and capable of understanding, it must rely on these six matters together to accomplish wisdom.
The King said: "Excellent, excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"When a person performs good deeds, is the merit obtained great?
When they perform evil deeds, is the calamity incurred great?"
Nāgasena said: "When a person performs good deeds, they obtain great merit; when they perform evil deeds, they incur only slight calamity.
If a person commits evil but repents their transgressions day after day, for that reason their offenses diminish daily."
"When others perform good deeds, they rejoice in their hearts day and night; for this reason, they obtain great merit. Nāgasena said:
"In the past, when the Buddha was in the world, there was a man in that country who had no hands or feet. He dug up lotus flowers and brought them as an offering to the Buddha."
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"This boy, Hand-and-Foot-Digger, for ninety-one kalpas thereafter shall no longer enter the hells, nor the realms of animals or hungry ghosts; he shall attain rebirth in the heavens."
"When their lifespan in heaven comes to an end, they return again to become humans.
For this reason, I know that by performing even small good deeds, one obtains great merit.
When a person commits evil, they repent of it themselves; as the days pass, those transgressions are extinguished and exhausted.
"Therefore, I know that when a person commits a transgression, the calamity is small.
The King said: "Excellent, excellent!"
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"Between a wise person who commits evil and a foolish person who commits evil, which of these two incurs the greater karmic retribution?
Nāgasena replied:
"The fool who commits evil incurs great calamity; the wise person who commits evil incurs small calamity.
The King said, "I do not understand what Nāgasena has said."
The king said,
"The law of my kingdom is such that when a high minister commits an offense, the punishment is severe, whereas when a commoner commits an offense,

the punishment is light. Therefore, I know that when a wise person commits an evil deed, the calamity they receive is great, while when a fool commits an evil deed, the calamity they receive is small."

Nāgasena asked the king, "Suppose there were a piece of heated iron on the ground; one person knew it was heated iron while another did not, yet both went forward to grasp the heated iron. Which of the two would suffer greater burns to their hands?"
The King said, "I do not know; the hand would have rotted extensively. Nāgasena said:
"The fool commits evil and cannot repent of it himself; therefore, his calamity is great.
The wise person commits evil but knows it was not what ought to be done; he repents his transgressions daily, and therefore his calamity is small."
The king said, "Excellent, excellent!
The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"Is there anyone who can maintain this body and fly upward as far as the seventh Brahma-heaven, or reach the land of Uttarakuru, or go to whatever place they desire?"
Nāgasena said, "I can. The King asked:
"How could one carry this body to the seventh Brahma-heaven, or to the land of Uttarakuru, or to wherever one wishes to go?
Nāgasena asked the king:
"Do you not recall, Sire, when you were young, jumping across a space of ten feet while playing?"
The king said,
“When I was young, I intended to leap, and I leaped more than a fathom across the ground. Nāgasena said:
"One who has attained the Way may wish to leap as far as the seventh heaven, and it is likewise when reaching the land of Uttarakuru.
The king said, "Excellent, excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"Your various śramaṇas say that there are bones four thousand li long.
What kind of bodily bone is four thousand li long?"
Nāgasena asked:
"Your Majesty, have you ever heard that in the great ocean there is a large fish named Timi, whose body is twenty-eight thousand li in length?
The King replied:
"It is so. Such a thing exists; I have heard it before. Nāgasena said:
“Regarding these twenty-eight thousand *li* of fish, their rib bones are four thousand *li* long; why does Your Majesty find this strange?
The King again asked Nāgasena:
“You śramaṇas say that you are able to stop the movement of the breath.”
The king asked, "How can one cut off the breath?
Nāgasena asked the king:
“Have you ever heard of Zhì?
The king replied,
“I have heard of him.”
Nāgasena asked: "Does Your Majesty consider that [the self] resides within the human body?
The King replied:
"I believe that one's aspirations lie within the human body. Nāgasena said:
"Your Majesty considers such people fools; those who cannot restrain their bodies and speech cannot uphold the sūtras and precepts, and such persons do not even delight in their own bodies."

Nāgasena said: "As for those who practice the Way, they are able to restrain their bodies, able to restrain their speech, and able to uphold the sūtras and precepts; when they can unify their minds and attain the four dhyānas, they are then no longer subject to breathing."
The king said, "Excellent, excellent!
The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"If one calls it 'ocean,' is it because this water is named 'ocean' that it is called so?
Or is it called 'ocean' for some other reason? Nāgasena replied:
"The reason people call it the 'ocean' is that water and salt are each half of its composition; for this reason, it is called the ocean.
The King asked Nāgasena again, "For what reason is the ocean entirely salty, with a taste like salt?"

Nāgasena said: "The reason the seawater is salty is that it has been consumed by livestock for a long time, and many fish, turtles, and insects have all soaked in the water; therefore, it has become salty."
The king said, "Excellent, excellent!
The king then questioned Nāgasena again.
“Once a person has attained the Way, can they contemplate all profound matters?
Nāgasena replied:
"Indeed. Once a person has attained the Way, they are able to contemplate all profound matters.
The Buddha’s sutras are most profound; they encompass knowledge of all things, which are immeasurable, and all such matters are evaluated through wisdom."
The king said, “Excellent, excellent!
The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"Are these three things—man, consciousness, and nature—the same, or are they each different?
Nāgasena replied, "Man and consciousness give rise to awareness; wisdom understands the Path; and nature is empty space, wherein no person exists."
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"People say one has 'attained a person. What is it that constitutes having attained a person?

Now, the eyes see forms, the ears hear sounds, the nose smells fragrances and odors, the mouth knows tastes, the body perceives what is soft or coarse, and the mind knows good and evil matters; what is it that constitutes having attained a person?"
Nāgasena asked the king:
"Suppose one were to remove the pupils from one's eyes; would one's vision then become more vast and far-reaching?
Or suppose one were to tear open and enlarge one's ears; would one's hearing then become more vast and far-reaching?"
If one were to enlarge the nostrils, would one’s perception of fragrances thereby increase?
If one were to widen the mouth, would one’s discernment of flavors thereby increase?
If one were to strip away the skin and flesh, would one thereby gain a more certain knowledge of what is coarse or soft?
“If one were to remove that intention, would the remaining thoughts be many?
The King replied, “No.”
Nāgasena said: "What the Buddha has accomplished is exceedingly difficult; what the Buddha knows is exceedingly subtle.
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"What is it that he has done which is so exceedingly difficult, and what is it so exceedingly marvelous?
Nāgasena replied, "The Buddha can know things within a person's belly that the eyes cannot see; he can fully understand them all."

One is able to understand the phenomena of the eye, the phenomena of the ear, the phenomena of the nose, the phenomena of the mouth, the phenomena of the body, the phenomena of the tongue, the phenomena of the mind, and the phenomena of consciousness.

Nāgasena said: "If a person were to take up seawater in his mouth, would he be able to distinguish that the water in his mouth belongs to such-and-such a spring, such-and-such a stream, or such-and-such a river?"
The king said,
"When all the waters merge into one, it is difficult to know them individually. Nāgasena said:
"The deeds performed by the Buddha are most difficult; he is able to discern them all.
Yet, though humans and spirits cannot see them, there are six things within the human body that are invisible. Nāgasena said:

"Therefore, the Buddha understands them: from the mental intention to what is seen by the eyes; from the mental intention to what is heard by the ears; from the mental intention to what is smelled by the nose; from the mental intention to the knowledge of flavors by the mouth; from the mental intention to the knowledge of suffering, pleasure, cold, warmth, roughness, and hardness by the body; and from the mental intention toward whatever object it is directed—the Buddha knows, discerns, and understands them all."
The King said, "Excellent, excellent! Nāgasena said:
"It is already midnight; I wish to depart.
The king immediately commanded his attendant ministers:
"Take four pieces of fine cotton cloth, soak them in oil-seed oil, and use them as torches to escort Nāgasena back."
"Serve Nāgasena as you would serve my own person.
The ministers at his side all replied,
"We shall obey your instructions."
The King said, "If one can obtain a teacher such as Nāgasena and become a disciple such as I, one may attain the Way swiftly.

Whatever the King asked, Nāgasena answered each matter accordingly; the King was greatly delighted and immediately took ten thousand pieces of fine clothing from his inner treasury to present to Nāgasena.
The King said to Nāgasena:
"From this day forward, I wish for you, Nāgasena, to dine together with eight hundred bhikṣus within the palace, and that you may take from the King whatever you desire."
Nāgasena replied to the king, "I am a man of the Way; I have almost no desires.
The king said to Nāgasena:
"One should protect oneself, and one should also protect my person.
Nāgasena asked: "In what way should one protect oneself and protect the King's person?"
The king replied,
"I fear people will debate and call me stingy;
though Nāgasena has resolved all my doubts, he has not yet granted me anything."
"Or perhaps people will say:
'Nāgasena could not resolve the King's doubts; therefore, the King does not grant him a reward.
The King said to Nāgasena:
"The recipient shall cause me to obtain merit, and Nāgasena shall likewise protect his reputation.
The King said:
"It is like a lion within a golden cage; though confined therein, it always has the desire to depart."
"Now, although I am within the royal palace and its precincts, my heart finds no joy; I wish to abandon the kingdom and depart to practice the Way.
When the King had finished speaking, Nāgasena returned to the Buddhist monastery.
Just as Nāgasena had departed, the king thought to himself:
"What matters did I ask Nāgasena about? What matters has he explained for me?"
The king thought to himself:
"I hope that Nāgasena has not failed to understand my meaning.
Nāgasena, upon returning to the monastery, also thought to himself:
"What matter will the King ask me?
What matter shall I, in turn, answer the King?
Nāgasena thought to himself.
"What the King asks, I shall fully understand.

Thinking these words until dawn, the next day Nāgasena donned his *kāṣāya* robe and, carrying his alms bowl, went directly into the palace and took his seat upon the dais. After the King had paid homage to Nāgasena, he withdrew to sit at one side.
The King said to Nāgasena:
“Just as you had departed, I thought to myself:
‘What question shall I ask Nāgasena?’”
"What words will Nāgasena reply to me?
I thought to myself again:
"I hope that when I question Nāgasena, he will not fail to understand my meaning."
"Recalling these words with joy, I lay down peacefully until dawn. Nāgasena said:
"As I was returning home, I too reflected to myself:"
"What matter will the King ask me about?
What matter shall I explain to the King?
Then I further reflected to myself:
"Whatever the King asks, I shall immediately explain it for him.
For this reason, may you rejoice until dawn.
When he had finished speaking, Nāgasena wished to depart; the King then rose and paid homage to Nāgasena.
*Nāgasena Bhikṣu Sūtra*, Scroll II. [Sanskrit: *Nāgasena*] (Ārya) [Mahā], [Sanskrit: *Nāgasena*]. First, the suffering and affliction; then, the one who surpasses the Buddha.
